title: His son Abraham
hook: Abraham Maimonides wrote of intense inner devotion

segments.voice: Yesterday's line: two ways of thinking. The Ramban read the same verses as Maimonides and argued, toward the plain story and a hidden depth. Did a second reader answer your question differently? Day one thousand one hundred sixty-five.

The child of a famous parent hears one question again and again: are you going to be just like your father? Maimonides had a son named Abraham. He inherited his father's books, his father's critics, and, tradition says, his father's role leading the Jews of Egypt. But when Abraham sat down to write his own great book, it wasn't another law code and it wasn't another Guide. It was about the inside of a person at prayer. Today's word is the son, and the path he chose.
screen: `JUST LIKE YOUR FATHER?` → `THE BOOKS, THE CRITICS, THE ROLE.` → `HIS OWN BOOK.`

segments.voice: His son Abraham. Turn his path four ways. First, the father's line. In his law code, Maimonides wrote that prayer without kavanah, without intention, is not prayer. A person should clear the mind, he says, and see themselves as standing before God. That's a law, stated in a sentence. Second, the son's book. Abraham Maimonides wrote a large work in Judeo-Arabic, its title often given as a complete guide for the servants of God. It takes that sentence about intention and turns it into a whole way of life: humility, generosity, patience, solitude, nights awake in prayer. He calls it a path, and the people walking it he calls hasidim, the devoted. Third, the neighbors he noticed. Abraham lived among Muslims and saw the discipline of the Sufi mystics. He wrote that some of their practices looked like what the ancient prophets of Israel once did, practices he felt his own people had lost. So he urged ways of praying with the whole body: bowing low, kneeling, standing in ordered rows, raising the hands. Some in his community pushed back against these changes, and the argument was real. Fourth, a verse at the center. A verse from the Psalms puts this kind of devotion in a line: "I have set the LORD always before me." The father gave reasons for faith and a code for living it. The son asked what it feels like from inside, when a person actually means the words. Both are Maimonides. One wrote the law of intention. The other tried to live inside it.
screen: `PRAYER WITHOUT INTENTION IS NOT PRAYER.` · `A GUIDE FOR THE SERVANTS OF GOD.` · `BOWING, KNEELING, STANDING IN ROWS.` · `THE LORD ALWAYS BEFORE ME.` · then, large: `THE SON'S PATH.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes, or lower them, and let the breath come and go. Take one line you already know by heart. If you pray, it might be the Shema, or a line from a psalm, or "I have set the LORD always before me." If you don't pray, choose one true sentence of thanks. Now say it once, slowly, and mean each word as it passes. Not faster. Not twice. Once, with your whole attention. Then sit in the quiet it leaves behind. The bell holds the time.
His son Abraham. Abraham Maimonides, who took his father's law of intention in prayer and wrote a whole path of inner devotion around it. Today's word.
Your line: the son's path. Today, say one thing you usually rush, a blessing, a thank you, a goodbye, and mean it all the way through. Day one thousand one hundred sixty-five.

howItsDone: Jewish prayer asks for kavanah, intention, and some people slow down at key lines, such as the first verse of the Shema, to say them with full attention.

original.note: Hebrew: intention, the inner focus a person brings to prayer and to commandments.

trapdoor: what you thought: the son of a famous philosopher became a philosopher.
what it means: Abraham Maimonides wrote about inner devotion, a path of prayer with intention.
what a scholar hears: the Kifayat al-'Abidin in Judeo-Arabic, building on Hilchot Tefillah 4:16, with pietist practices he saw echoed among the Sufis.

notes: Hilchot Tefillah 4:15–16 (prayer without kavanah is not prayer; clear the mind and see oneself standing before the Shechinah) paraphrased. Please confirm.
Abraham Maimonides' leadership of Egyptian Jewry (Nagid) is framed as 'tradition says'; please confirm and firm up if appropriate.

Kifayat al-'Abidin: title rendering, Judeo-Arabic language, the themes listed, the term hasidim, his remarks that Sufi practices resembled those of Israel's prophets, and the practices he urged (prostration, kneeling, rows, raising hands) and the opposition they met are all paraphrased from standard accounts. Please verify each against the text.
Shema is named as one possible line 'if you pray'; no new prayer written.
Psalm 16:8 JPS 1917: confirm 'I have set the LORD always before me'.
Original: כַּוָּנָה stress on the final syllable; confirm transliteration.
